lead: An antenna is qualified by measuring three things: its gain, its pattern (where the beam points, how wide it is, how high the sidelobes are) and its polarization. All three need the test antenna to sit in the far field of a source antenna, on a range that keeps reflections out of the measurement. Gain is found by comparing the test antenna with a standard horn of known gain, the pattern by turning the test antenna and recording the received power, and the polarization by turning a linear probe or by using two crossed probes.
prereq: You need: gain, directivity, the radiation pattern and polarization from the antenna fundamentals topic, and the standard gain horn from aperture and horn antennas.

sections.h3: The far-field condition and the test range

blocks.text: Near an antenna the wavefront arriving from a source is curved, so the test aperture is not lit in phase, the nulls fill in and the gain reads low. The usual rule keeps the extra path at the aperture edge below λ/16:

blocks.where: R is the distance between the phase centres of the two antennas in m; D is the largest dimension of the test antenna in m (when the source antenna is also large, use the larger of the two, or check both); λ is the wavelength in m. R must also be many times D and λ.

blocks.text: A 0.3 m horn at 10 GHz needs only 6 m; a 3 m dish at 6 GHz needs 360 m, which is why big antennas are measured outdoors or by other means. Outdoor ranges raise both antennas on towers so that the ground reflection is weak. Anechoic chambers line a room with pyramidal absorber so that walls reflect almost nothing and the weather stays out. A compact range uses a large reflector to make a plane wave inside a small room, and a near-field scanner moves a probe close to the antenna and computes the far field by a transform.

Reflections that reach the receiver add to or cancel the direct wave and ripple the measured pattern. Keep the path clear, use absorber, and where the receiver allows it, time-gate the direct pulse. Every cable, attenuator and connector between the antenna and the instrument must be the same in both halves of a comparison, or measured and subtracted, on the transmit side as well as the receive side.

Gain by substitution (gain transfer): a fixed source antenna transmits. The receiver records Pstd with a standard gain horn of known gain Gstd at the test point, then Ptest with the test antenna in the same place, same polarization and same cable. With powers in dBm and gains in dBi:
G<sub>test</sub> and G<sub>std</sub> in dBi; P<sub>test</sub> and P<sub>std</sub> in dBm. More received power means more gain.

Two-antenna method: with two identical antennas R apart, the Friis equation gives each gain directly: 2G = Pr − Pt + 20 log(4πR/λ), all in dB. Three-antenna method: with three different antennas measured in pairs, the three pair sums G1 + G2, G1 + G3 and G2 + G3 are three equations for three unknowns, so no standard is needed. Both need an accurate R and the far-field condition.

For a pattern cut, the test antenna (usually receiving, by reciprocity the same pattern as transmitting) turns on a positioner about its phase centre while the receiver records power against angle. The E-plane cut contains the electric field and the beam axis; the H-plane cut contains the magnetic field and the beam axis. Normalize to the peak, plot in dB and read the HPBW, the first nulls and the sidelobe level. Repeating with the source turned 90° gives the cross-polar pattern.

For polarization, a linear probe is spun about the line joining the antennas. A linearly polarized test antenna gives a deep minimum when the probe is crossed; a circular one gives a constant reading; an elliptical one swings between E<sub>max</sub> and E<sub>min</sub>. Two crossed probes measure the two components and their phase: equal amplitudes 90° apart give circular polarization, and which component leads fixes the sense, right-hand or left-hand. Checking against a known right-hand and left-hand circular horn confirms it.
AR is the axial ratio: 1 (0 dB) for circular, infinite for linear. A received-power swing of 6 dB as the probe turns means AR = 2.
A linear antenna turned ψ away from a linear source receives only cos²ψ of the matched power, the polarization loss factor: 30° costs 1.25 dB, 45° costs 3 dB and 90° in principle everything.

examples.question: A 10 GHz test antenna has a largest dimension of 0.3 m. On a range a standard horn of 15 dBi gives a received power of −30 dBm; the test antenna in its place, with the same cable, gives −25 dBm. Find the minimum range length and the test gain. What would the answer be if the test antenna had been connected through an extra adaptor of 0.4 dB loss that was not used with the horn?
steps: R ≥ 2D²/λ = 2 × 0.09/0.03 = 6 m between the phase centres.
P<sub>test</sub> − P<sub>std</sub> = −25 − (−30) = +5 dB, so G<sub>test</sub> = 15 + 5 = 20 dBi.
With the extra adaptor, the −25 dBm reading is 0.4 dB lower than the antenna delivered, so the true gain is 20 + 0.4 = 20.4 dBi; ignoring it would under-read by 0.4 dB.
examples.answer: R ≥ 6 m and G<sub>test</sub> = 20 dBi; with the uncorrected 0.4 dB adaptor the true gain is 20.4 dBi.

examples.question: Two identical horns face each other 6 m apart at 10 GHz. The transmitter delivers 0 dBm to one horn and the other receives −30 dBm. Find the gain of each horn. A third horn is then measured with each of them: the pair sums are G<sub>1</sub> + G<sub>2</sub> = 38.0 dB, G<sub>1</sub> + G<sub>3</sub> = 35.0 dB and G<sub>2</sub> + G<sub>3</sub> = 33.0 dB. Find all three gains.
steps: Free-space loss: 20 log(4πR/λ) = 20 log(4π × 6/0.03) = 20 log 2513 = 68.0 dB.
Friis in dB: P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub> + 2G − 68.0, so 2G = −30 − 0 + 68.0 = 38.0 dB and G = 19.0 dBi for each identical horn.
Three-antenna method: add all three sums: 2(G<sub>1</sub> + G<sub>2</sub> + G<sub>3</sub>) = 106.0, so the total is 53.0 dB.
examples.answer: Each identical horn has 19.0 dBi; the three-antenna method gives 20.0, 18.0 and 15.0 dBi without any standard horn.

traps: Measuring inside 2D²/λ. The pattern is a near-field one: nulls fill and the gain reads low.
Subtracting the wrong way in substitution. More received power means more gain: G<sub>test</sub> = G<sub>std</sub> + (P<sub>test</sub> − P<sub>std</sub>).
Forgetting that cables count on both sides. Any loss used with one antenna and not the other enters the answer in full, whether it is on the transmit or the receive side.
Swapping the E-plane and H-plane cuts. The E-plane contains the electric field vector of the antenna’s main polarization.
Giving linear polarization an axial ratio of 0 dB. Circular is 0 dB (AR = 1); linear is infinite.

quiz.q: State the far-field condition and define each symbol.
quiz.a: R ≥ 2D²/λ: R is the distance between the phase centres, D the largest antenna dimension and λ the wavelength, all in metres.

quiz.q: What does an anechoic chamber remove, and what does multipath do to a pattern?
quiz.a: It absorbs wall reflections and keeps out weather and outside signals. Multipath adds to or cancels the direct wave, giving ripples and false or filled nulls.

quiz.q: At 5 GHz a test antenna is 0.5 m across. Find the minimum range length.
A standard horn of 12 dBi gives −40 dBm; the test antenna gives −37 dBm. Find the test gain.
A spinning linear probe shows a 6 dB swing in received power. Find the axial ratio.
quiz.a: The field swings by 6/20 decades: AR = 10<sup>6/20</sup> = 2.0, that is 6 dB.

quiz.q: A student measures at R = D²/λ and finds filled nulls and a low gain. Explain and correct.
quiz.a: At D²/λ the edge of the aperture sees the source λ/8 farther than the centre, twice the λ/16 allowed, so the aperture is not in phase. Move to at least 2D²/λ and clear reflections.

quiz.q: Crossed probes show equal amplitudes, with the vertical component leading the horizontal by 90°. What do you report, and how do you confirm the sense?
quiz.a: Circular polarization with AR = 1 (0 dB); the sign of the 90° fixes the sense. Confirm by receiving with a known right-hand and left-hand circular horn: the matching one gives the higher reading.

beyond: Not for the exam. Spherical near-field scanners and compact ranges measure large satellite and radar antennas in rooms a few metres across. Phones and 5G modules with antennas built into the radio have no test connector, so they are measured over the air for total radiated power and receiver sensitivity. Search for compact antenna test range, spherical near-field measurement and OTA testing.

figure.caption: Gain by substitution, as in the first worked example: a fixed source horn transmits, and the receiver reads −30 dBm with the 15 dBi standard horn and then −25 dBm with the test antenna in its place. The 5 dB difference gives 20 dBi. The range length R, at least 2D²/λ = 6 m here, is taken between the phase centres.
